disclaimer.1: This tool helps you compare. It shows which party's ideas are closest to yours. It does not tell you how to vote. You decide.
disclaimer.3: This tool is independent of all parties. It compares your answers with parties' promises and records. It is a starting point, not a recommendation. Parties were still announcing promises as of October 10, so check for updates. Party names and logos belong to the parties.
disclaimer.5: Independent voter-information tool. Scores reflect published 2026 commitments as of October 10, 2026, weighted against the 2016-2026 governing and legislative record where the two conflict. CentreBC released a full platform on October 10 with its own costing, not independently checked; the Greens' full platform was still pending; the other parties campaign on rolling announcements without a complete costed platform. Low-confidence positions rest on prior-leader statements, 2024 platforms or silence. Party names and logos are trademarks of their owners, shown for identification only. Not an endorsement.

method_summary.1: You pick answers. Each answer is close to some groups and far from others. We add it up and show the closest group.
method_summary.3: Each option scores 0 (opposite) to 4 (match) for every party. Your match is the percentage of the maximum you could score. Important questions count more; skips and 'not sure' do not count. Questions where a party has no published position are left out of its score. Partly agreeing with everyone tends to favour centrist parties. Near ties show as close. Where record and words conflict, the record decides.
method_summary.5: Alignment(P) = sum(w_q x s_q(P)) / sum(w_q x 4) over answered questions, where s_q(P) is the chosen option's 0-4 score for P and w_q the importance weight (low 0.5, medium 1, high 2). Skipped questions (including 'not sure') leave both sums. Questions where P has no published position leave both sums for P only. Inferred positions use an adjacent stated policy. Close: top two whole-number percentages within 3 points. Family score: mean of members' percentages per party, plus an adults-only mean (levels 3 to 5). For candidates, local questions count double on top of importance; no candidate-specific adjustment. Scores were set from the cited sources with an AI assistant (Claude) and checked by separate review passes; every score, rationale and source is public at github.com/vinistoisr/bc-vote-helper. Reading level changes wording only.

display_rules.option_order: Shuffle the display order of options for every respondent and every family member. Option ids and scores never change. Store the order shown with the answers so a result can be audited. If a fixed order is needed for print, alternate the direction of the spectrum from one question to the next so no side is first more often.
display_rules.not_sure: Every question carries an 'I'm not sure / skip' choice. It counts as a skip: the question leaves both the numerator and the denominator for every party.
display_rules.no_position: When party_positions[party].no_position is true, the party has no published position on that question. Leave the question out of that party's numerator and denominator and show 'No published position' in the per-issue view. The option scores for that cell are placeholders (2) only.
display_rules.inferred: When party_positions[party].basis is 'inferred', the score comes from an adjacent stated policy, not a statement on the question. Tag it 'inferred' in the per-issue view.
display_rules.ties: When the first and second party are within 3 points, present the result as close rather than naming a single match.
display_rules.drivers: On the results page, list the three questions that contributed most to the top party's lead so users can see what decided the match.
display_rules.family: Family score is the mean of members' percentages. Show an adults-only mean (members who answered at levels 3 to 5) beside the all-members mean and label both.
display_rules.party_positions_levels: Party position text exists at levels 1, 3 and 5. Show level 1 text at level 2 and level 5 text at level 4.
display_rules.importance_default: Default importance is medium for every question; users change it per question.

parties.name: BC New Democratic Party
parties.leader_note: Premier since November 2022; former Attorney General and housing minister.

one_liner.1: The party that has run the government since 2017. It wants government to run more programs and set rules to help people.
one_liner.3: In government since 2017. Uses provincial power actively (housing taxes, zoning rules, big projects) and asks higher earners to pay more, but has reversed several policies under pressure.
one_liner.5: Governing since 2017. Record: speculation and vacancy tax (2018), Bills 44 and 47 density mandates (2023), Bill 36 Surrey police transition (2023), consumer carbon tax repeal (2025), decriminalization ended (2026), Budget 2026 deficit $13.3B (revised $13.8B). 2026: +2 points on brackets above $190,405, 24.5% above $1M, 10 c/L fuel tax cut, grocery margin caps, ICBC freeze to 2030, 20 clinics.

record_summary.3: The NDP has governed for nine years. It is building the Surrey-Langley SkyTrain and a new Surrey hospital, and it brought in $10-a-day child care, then froze new spaces. It taxed empty homes, ordered Surrey's switch to a city police force and passed the law on Indigenous rights (DRIPA). It later ended the drug decriminalization trial, scrapped the carbon tax on fuel and paused a promised $1,000 rebate. The deficit reached its highest dollar amount ever, and credit agencies lowered BC's rating in 2026.
record_summary.5: Party-line votes: Bill 45 (43-39, 2018), Bill 36 (56-27, 2023), Bills 44 and 46 (2023), Bill 7 (48-44), Bills 14 and 15 (46-46, Speaker's vote, 2025), Bill 3 budget measures (46-42). Reversals: Bill 7 Part 4 withdrawn, $1,000 rebate paused, carbon tax to $0, decriminalization not renewed, witnessed-only safer supply, EV mandate dropped, DRIPA suspension bill withdrawn, vehicle levy ruled out. Budget 2026: lowest bracket 5.06% to 5.60%, indexation frozen 2027-2030. Four downgrades in 2026.

parties.name: Conservative Party of British Columbia
parties.leader_note: Interim leader since September 20, 2026, after Kerry-Lynne Findlay resigned; party rules bar an interim leader from seeking the permanent job.
parties.seats_note: 28 at dissolution on September 22, 2026 per Wikipedia (secondary; CP24 reported 24 on September 20); 36 after seven CentreBC MLAs and one independent returned when the writ dropped. Won 44 in 2024.

one_liner.1: The main party trying to replace the government. It wants lower taxes, fewer rules for business and more gas and mining jobs.
one_liner.3: Opposition since 2024. Promises a $1,000 income tax cut and no new taxes; would repeal DRIPA and SOGI 123, end safe supply, expand mandatory treatment and double gas production. Four leaders in a year; no costed plan.
one_liner.5: Opposition since 2024 (44 seats). 2026: basic personal amount to $32,000 (about $1,050 each; uncosted; outside estimate $2.5B a year), no new taxes, repeal DRIPA and SOGI 123, end safe supply, mandatory treatment, 250 police, 500 RCMP, 50 prosecutors, double gas output by 2032, 120 Day Permitting Act, ICBC hybrid tort, portable LTC funding. No deficit target or balance date.

record_summary.3: Its 2024 calls to end the carbon tax and for mandatory treatment and bail reform preceded NDP action. Opposed nearly all NDP bills. Most MLAs backed first reading of gender identity and Human Rights Code repeal bills, citing courtesy. Many backed DRIPA as BC Liberals. Four leaders since December 2025.
record_summary.5: Nay on Bills 7, 14, 15, 32 (Mental Health Amendment), the Supply Act 2025 and Bill 3 (2026); non-confidence amendment lost 44-48. Yea at first reading on independents' property rights (40-48), gender identity (38-49) and Human Rights Code repeal (37-50) bills. BC Liberals, including Rustad, backed DRIPA (82-0 in committee, 2019). Rustad removed December 2025, then Halford (interim), Findlay (113 days), Doerkson (interim). 2024 pledges (rent rebate, Bill 44 repeal, balance in two terms) dropped.

parties.name: BC Green Party
parties.leader_note: Leader since September 2025; does not hold a seat. Two MLAs at dissolution.

one_liner.1: A smaller party. It wants to protect nature, tax the richest people more, and spend more on child care, transit and homes.
one_liner.3: Two seats. A wealth tax on fortunes over $50 million would fund free child care, free youth and senior transit, and non-market housing. Would strengthen DRIPA and SOGI 123, restore decriminalization, stop new fossil fuel projects. Revenue estimate method unpublished.
one_liner.5: Two MLAs; 8.2% in 2024. Fair Share Act: one-time 5-20% levy on net wealth above $50M, then 2-5% yearly (party estimate $22.2B, then $5.4B; uncosted). 26,000 non-market homes yearly, vacancy control, free child care by 2031, free transit under 25 and over 65, health centre per riding, PR bill within 100 days, decriminalization, no new fossil fuel development. Platform pending.

record_summary.3: Backed NDP confidence votes under written deals (2017-2020, 2024-2026), gaining the corporate and union donation ban and the 2018 voting referendum. Opposed the fast-track laws and the carbon tax repeal. Voted for the 2026 budget at second reading, against at third. Left the deal in February 2026, citing stalled promises.
record_summary.5: CASA 2017-2020: Bill 3 donation ban and 2018 PR referendum (lost 61.3 to 38.7). Yea on Bill 45 spec tax (2018) after amendments; nay on Bills 44 and 46 (2023); yea on Supply Act 2025; nay on Bills 14 and 15 (2025), the carbon tax repeal and Bill 3 at third reading (2026); nay on Armstrong's gender identity, Human Rights Code repeal and drug recovery bills. NDP accord (December 2024) not renewed February 9, 2026.

parties.name: CentreBC
parties.leader_note: Named leader September 22, 2026; the party's only incumbent MLA (Surrey-Cloverdale, running in Surrey South). Fourth leader since the party formed in March 2025.
parties.seats_note: 8 at dissolution per Wikipedia (secondary); 7 returned to the Conservatives when the writ dropped, leaving 1.

one_liner.1: A new party in the political centre. It wants a cost on every promise, a slow return to a balanced budget, and to replace the law on Indigenous rights with treaty deals.
one_liner.3: New centre-right party, 35 candidates. Its October 10 platform, costed by the party, cuts the bottom tax rate, balances the budget by 2034-35 with 10,000 fewer public jobs by attrition, keeps ICBC and health care public, adds 650 treatment beds and 500 RCMP, and would repeal DRIPA for a treaty-based law. Seven of its eight MLAs rejoined the Conservatives at the election call.
one_liner.5: Registered March 2025; leaders Kirkpatrick, Bernier, Milobar, Sturko (September 2026). Platform October 10 ($13.7B over four years, party costing): first bracket 5.06%, renter's credit $600, balance 2034/35 in law, Independent Budget Officer, 10,000 positions by attrition; repeal DRIPA and s. 8.1 for a treaty law (reverses its August stance); industrial carbon pricing kept, 2030 target reset to 20%; 650 treatment beds, involuntary assessments; 500 RCMP, 60 Crown; ICBC public, rate cap; 20,000 child care spaces, 25,000 seats; Surrey Memorial tower. Silent on SOGI 123, zoning law, safer supply, electoral reform.

record_summary.3: No governing record. At the election call, then-leader Milobar and seven of eight MLAs rejoined the Conservatives. Sturko was elected in 2024 as a Conservative on a platform to repeal DRIPA and remove SOGI 123, left that caucus in 2025, and opposed gender identity and Human Rights Code repeal bills.
record_summary.5: Sturko (elected 2022 as BC Liberal; Conservative 2024; removed from caucus September 22, 2025) voted nay at first reading on the Gender Ideology and Child Protection Act and the Human Rights Code Repeal Act (February 2026); chaired the police complaints committee. As MLA she introduced Mental Health Act amendments on family contact before involuntary admission and opposed non-medical safer supply. The October 10 platform supersedes statements by prior leaders Kirkpatrick and Bernier; on DRIPA it reverses Bernier's August 2026 'no repeal' position.

parties.name: OneBC
parties.leader_note: Co-founded the party in June 2025 after being removed from the Conservative caucus in March 2025 over posts about residential school burial claims; removed and reinstated as leader by the party board in December 2025.

one_liner.1: A small new party. It wants much lower taxes, fewer rules, and to end some laws it sees as unfair.
one_liner.3: New right-wing party, about 34 candidates. Would cut every tax rate by 25%, balance in four years, repeal DRIPA and SOGI 123, end safe supply and consumption sites, allow private care alongside public, open car insurance to competition. All uncosted.
one_liner.5: Founded 2025 (Brodie, Armstrong). Repeal DRIPA, void UNDRIP, end voluntary land transfers, seek Indian Act repeal; 25% cut to every bracket including corporate; PST down 2 points; balance in four years; end safe supply, consumption sites; involuntary rehab; private care, HPOA repeal; end ICBC monopoly, no-fault; repeal SOGI 123; Parental Bill of Rights; end mail-in and early voting. All uncosted.

record_summary.3: No governing record. Its MLAs' bills to restrict youth gender transition, ban land acknowledgements and protect property rights were all defeated. Its board removed and reinstated leader Brodie in December 2025. It is standing aside for eight Conservatives who share its SOGI views.
record_summary.5: Private members' bills: puberty blocker and pronoun bill defeated 48-40 before first reading (October 2025); Land Acknowledgement Prohibition Act 88-5 (October 2025); Property Rights Protection Act 40-48 (October 2025); DRIPA repeal bill 44-47 (April 2026, unverified against Hansard). Board removed Brodie December 13, 2025, reinstated December 21. Brent Chapman crossed from the Conservatives September 22, 2026; sources conflict on whether that restored official party status; he is not running. Not running against eight named Conservatives.

prompt.1: Food, gas and rent cost more now. How should the government help people with costs?
prompt.2: Groceries, gas and rent cost more than they used to. How should the province help families pay for them?
prompt.3: Cost of living is the top issue for BC voters. Which approach should the province take to make life more affordable?
prompt.4: Which cost-of-living approach should come first: tax cuts, price rules, more help for low incomes, or targeted credits and rate caps?
prompt.5: Which mix of cost-of-living measures should the province put first: broad tax cuts, price controls, income support, or targeted credits and rate caps?

context.1: Prices for food, gas and rent have gone up. Every party says it wants to make life cost less. Some want to cut taxes. Some want rules that keep prices down. Some want more help for people with low incomes.
context.2: Prices were 2.9% higher in July 2026 than a year before. Every party promises to make life more affordable, but they disagree on how. The province could cut taxes for everyone, limit some prices, give more money to people with the lowest incomes, or lower costs for businesses so they can charge less.
context.3: Cost of living is the top issue for BC voters. In 2025 the NDP government ended the consumer carbon tax, but it paused a $1,000 rebate, and in 2026 it raised the lowest tax rate. Every party promises relief in a different way. Some would cut income taxes for everyone. One would cap markups on gas and some groceries. Another would raise support for the poorest people. Others mix smaller tax cuts with limits on power and car insurance increases.
context.4: Cost of living ranks first for 56% of BC voters, according to an Ipsos poll. The minimum wage is $18.25 an hour and rises with inflation each year. In 2025 the NDP government paused a $1,000 grocery rebate, and in 2026 it raised the lowest income tax rate. The parties' price tags are hard to compare. The Conservative and OneBC tax cuts have no published cost. The Greens have not published how they estimated their wealth tax revenue, and CentreBC's cost figures are its own, not checked by anyone else.
context.5: Consumer prices rose 2.9% in the year to July 2026. The NDP government ended the consumer carbon tax in April 2025, and Budget 2026 raised the lowest income tax rate from 5.06% to 5.60%. The NDP proposes a 10-cent-a-litre fuel tax cut with a BC Utilities Commission cap on gas margins, caps on grocery margins, and a freeze on Insurance Corporation of British Columbia (ICBC) rates. The Conservatives would raise the basic personal amount, the income you earn tax-free, to $32,000. The Greens would raise income assistance to the poverty line and make transit free for people under 25 and over 65. CentreBC would return the lowest rate to 5.06%, raise the renter's credit to $600 and cap BC Hydro and ICBC increases. OneBC would cut every income tax rate by 25% and the provincial sales tax (PST) by two points.

text.3: OneBC would cut every income tax rate by 25%, including the rate companies pay, cut the provincial sales tax by two points, and end the public insurer's monopoly on car insurance. It has published no costing and no plans on prices or income assistance.

questions.scoring_rationale: Option a is the OneBC 25% cut and PST reduction (4); Conservatives share a broad cut but at a different scale and have not endorsed rate cuts of that size (2); CentreBC 1 (cuts one bracket modestly inside a legislated balance path and rejects cuts of this size); NDP and Green 0. Option b is the Conservative basic personal amount increase (4); OneBC 3 (would cut everyone's taxes, by a different instrument); CentreBC 2 (a broad income tax cut and no new taxes, but through the bottom rate, about half the size, and costed); NDP 1 (it did cut MSP and the carbon tax, but its 2026 direction is price regulation and a higher bottom rate); Green 0. Option c is the NDP 2026 package (4); Greens share the margin-disclosure instinct but not price caps (2); CentreBC 2 (caps Hydro and ICBC increases, a Crown-rate measure, but no grocery caps or fuel tax cut); Conservatives oppose price regulation but kept their own targeted PST-off-alcohol measure (1); OneBC 0. Option d is the Green plan (4); NDP 2 because it indexed the minimum wage and expanded benefits but froze child care and has no assistance pledge; CentreBC 1 (renter's credit and a caregiver benefit, no assistance or wage pledge, no wealth tax); Conservative and OneBC 0 (a non-refundable credit gives nothing to the lowest incomes). Option e is CentreBC's platform package (4): bottom rate to 5.06%, renter's credit $600, commuter credit, Hydro and ICBC caps, PST machinery relief; Conservatives 3 (voted against the bottom-rate rise, no new taxes, machinery PST exemption; no renter or rate-cap measures); OneBC 2 (broad tax cuts, no targeted measures); NDP 1 (it created the renter's credit and the ICBC freeze but enacted the rate rise the option reverses); Green 1 (renter support only). Option e was rewritten on October 10 from the earlier farm PST item, which the platform does not repeat; other parties' scores on it were kept. Symmetry check: Conservative on a (2) and OneBC on b (3) are within one point; NDP on e (1) and CentreBC on c (2) are within one point.

prompt.1: The province spends more money than it takes in. What should it do?
prompt.2: BC spends more than it takes in. How should it close the gap, and who should pay?
prompt.3: BC is spending far more than it takes in. How should it handle that, and who should pay more or less tax?

prompt.5: Which fiscal and tax path do you support for dealing with BC's $13.8 billion deficit?

context.1: The province spends more money than it takes in, so it borrows the rest. Borrowing costs extra because of interest. The province could spend less, raise some taxes, or keep borrowing to protect services.
context.2: BC's budget shows a deficit of about $13.8 billion, which means it spends that much more than it takes in. It borrows to cover the gap, and that adds interest costs. It can spend less, tax some people more, keep borrowing until the economy grows, or mix these.
context.3: BC's deficit, the gap between what it spends and what it takes in, is about $13.8 billion. That is a record in dollars. All four credit rating agencies lowered BC's rating in 2026. No party has a fully costed plan, so the parties' promises and price tags are hard to compare.
context.4: Budget 2026 projects a $13.8 billion deficit and debt rising to 37% of gross domestic product (GDP), the size of BC's economy, by 2028-29. The parties' plans differ in size. The NDP's higher tax on high incomes would raise about $1 billion a year. The Conservative tax cut would cost about $2.5 billion a year, by an outside estimate. The Greens estimate their wealth tax would raise $22.2 billion in its first year. CentreBC says its promises cost $13.7 billion over four years and would balance the budget in 2034-35. OneBC has not costed its cuts.
context.5: Budget 2026 projects a $13.8 billion deficit, with debt rising to 37.4% of gross domestic product (GDP) by 2028-29, and all four credit rating agencies downgraded BC this year. The NDP would add two points to the top two income tax brackets and charge 24.5% above $1 million (about $1 billion a year), and plans 15,000 fewer full-time-equivalent public positions. The Conservatives would raise the basic personal amount to $32,000 (about $2.5 billion a year, outside estimate) and set no deficit target. The Greens would tax wealth above $50 million ($22.2 billion in year one, party estimate). CentreBC would write a 2034-35 balanced budget into law, cut 10,000 positions as people leave and return the lowest rate to 5.06% ($13.7 billion over four years, party costing). OneBC would cut taxes 25% and balance in four years.

questions.scoring_rationale: Five options give each party a clear home. a = OneBC (4); Conservatives share deep tax cuts but have no balance date (2); CentreBC shares a legislated balance target but on an eight-year path with a modest cut (1). b = Conservative 2026 position (4); OneBC close (3); CentreBC 2 (no new taxes and a bracket cut, but a legislated balance date and party costing, which the option lacks); NDP and Green 0. c = CentreBC's platform (4): balance 2034/35 in law, Independent Budget Officer, attrition, bottom rate to 5.06%; Conservative 2 (fiscal rhetoric without a balance date or costing); NDP 1 because it enacted the bottom-rate increase the option reverses and has no balance date, although its fiscal plan also cuts FTEs; Green 1; OneBC 1 (a balance date, but four years and 25% cuts). d = NDP record and platform (4), including the enacted Budget 2026 measures; Green 3 because it voted for Supply 2025 and supports top-bracket increases while preferring a wealth tax; CentreBC 1 (also protects front-line services and cuts positions by attrition, but rejects the deficit path and the bracket increases). e = Green (4); NDP 1 for the school tax increase above $3M and top brackets, but it has adopted none of the option's instruments (wealth levy, windfall tax, royalty reform); others 0. The NDP-Green cross-scores are asymmetric on purpose: the Greens voted for the NDP's supply bill and support its bracket increases (3 on d), while the NDP has taken up none of the Green instruments (1 on e). Record over rhetoric: the NDP is scored on its enacted budget path, not only its campaign framing; the Conservatives are scored as uncosted because the 2024 balance pledge has been dropped. Symmetry: Conservative on a (2) and OneBC on b (3) are within one point.

prompt.1: Homes cost a lot to buy or rent. How should the government help?
prompt.2: Buying or renting a home in BC is expensive. How should the province help people afford housing?
prompt.3: What should the province do about the cost of housing?
prompt.4: Which housing approach should the province take: lower builder costs, taxes on empty homes, public building, faster approvals, or fewer rules?
prompt.5: Which mix of housing taxes, zoning rules, approval reforms and public building should the province pursue?

context.1: Homes cost a lot in BC. The government already charges extra tax on some empty homes. Some parties want fewer rules and fees so builders build more. Others want higher taxes on empty homes, or more homes built by government.
context.2: Since 2018 the province has taxed some homes left empty, and since 2023 it has made cities allow more homes on each lot. Rents in the Vancouver area are falling, but prices are still high and homelessness is up. Parties disagree on whether to cut builder costs, raise taxes on empty homes, or build more non-profit homes.
context.3: Housing ranks third among BC voters' concerns. The NDP government added a tax on homes left empty (the speculation and vacancy tax) in 2018 and a tax on homes resold quickly (the flipping tax) in 2025. A 2023 law makes cities allow up to four homes on most lots. Rents in the Vancouver area are easing, but homelessness is up. The parties disagree on whether to add more taxes and rules or remove them.
context.4: Metro Vancouver rents are falling and the rental vacancy rate is at a 30-year high, but prices are about 20% above 2016 levels and homelessness is up. The NDP government brought in the speculation and vacancy tax (SVT) on empty homes in 2018 and a flipping tax on quick resales in 2025. A 2023 law requires cities to allow up to four homes on most lots. In 2026 the NDP proposed doubling the SVT and taxing condos left unsold for over a year.
context.5: In Metro Vancouver, 3.7% of purpose-built rentals were vacant in 2025, and the benchmark home price was about $1.08 million in September 2026, down 5.5% from a year earlier. BC started 44,193 homes in 2025, and Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) forecasts fewer starts each year to 2028. The 2025 count found 5,232 homeless people, up 9%. The 2018 law creating the speculation and vacancy tax (Bill 45) passed 43 to 39, with the Greens for it and the BC Liberals against. The 2023 law letting up to four homes be built on most city lots (Bill 44) passed 45 to 29; BC United and the Greens voted against it. The 2023 law requiring more homes near transit (Bill 47) passed unanimously.

prompt.1: Many people cannot find a family doctor, and waiting rooms are full. What should change?
prompt.2: How should the province help people get a family doctor, emergency care and surgery sooner?
prompt.3: How should the province improve access to family doctors, emergency rooms and surgeries?
prompt.4: Which way of running and paying for health care should BC choose to cut waits and connect people to a doctor?
prompt.5: Which health care delivery and funding model do you support?

context.1: About one in four people in BC has no family doctor. Every party says health care should stay free. They disagree on who should run clinics and care homes, and on how to pay for more care.
context.2: About one in four people in BC has no regular family doctor or nurse practitioner, up from fewer than one in five in 2017. Every party says care should stay free for patients. They disagree on whether companies should run more care, and on how to pay for it.
context.3: Health care ranks second for BC voters. About one in four people has no regular family doctor or nurse practitioner, even after the NDP government changed how family doctors are paid in 2023. All parties say care should stay publicly funded. They differ on building more public clinics, paying non-government providers, allowing people to pay for faster care, and how to fund it all.
context.4: About 1.26 million people in BC (23%) have no regular family doctor or nurse practitioner, up from 18% in 2017, even though the NDP government brought in a new pay model for family doctors in 2023. The median wait from a doctor's referral to treatment is 32 weeks. A provincial law, the Medicare Protection Act, bars private clinics from charging patients for services the public plan covers.
context.5: In April 2026, 1,259,425 people (23%) had no regular primary care provider, compared with 897,000 (18.2%) in 2017. The family doctor payment model brought in in 2023 (LFP) connects about 4,000 people a week to a provider. The Fraser Institute puts the median wait from referral to treatment at 32.2 weeks. The government has put 73% of its minimum nurse-to-patient ratios in place, and the health budget is about $36 billion. The Medicare Protection Act bars extra-billing for services the public plan insures.

prompt.1: A BC law says provincial laws must respect Indigenous rights. What should happen to it?
prompt.2: A 2019 law says BC's laws should match Indigenous peoples' rights. What should happen to it now?
prompt.3: After a 2025 court ruling, what should BC do with the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act?

context.1: In 2019, BC lawmakers passed a law, with no one voting against, saying BC's laws should respect Indigenous peoples' rights. In 2025, a court said judges can check BC's laws against it. Parties disagree on what to do. First Nations keep their rights either way.
context.2: In 2019, BC passed a law promising to bring its laws in line with the United Nations declaration on Indigenous peoples' rights. In 2025, a court ruled that judges can check BC's laws against it. Supporters say the law builds fairness and trust. Critics say it leads to court cases and uncertainty. First Nations keep their rights either way.
context.3: The Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act passed in 2019 with no votes against. It commits BC to bring its laws in line with the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples. In 2025 the BC Court of Appeal ruled that this promise can be enforced in court. Repealing the law would not end the province's duty to consult First Nations or their land title cases, because those rest on section 35 of Canada's Constitution.
context.4: The Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act (DRIPA) passed unanimously in 2019. In December 2025, in a case brought by the Gitxaala Nation, the BC Court of Appeal held that courts can assess whether provincial laws are consistent with it. The Premier then proposed suspending the law for three years, but withdrew the bill in April 2026. In an Angus Reid poll in May 2026, 47% supported repeal and 33% opposed it. Repeal would not end the duty to consult, which rests on section 35 of the Constitution.
context.5: DRIPA (Bill 41) passed 82 to 0 in 2019. Under section 7 of the act, BC has signed consent agreements with First Nations, including the Tahltan in 2022 and one for Eskay Creek in January 2026. In Gitxaala v. British Columbia (2025 BCCA 430), the Court of Appeal ruled 2 to 1 that DRIPA duties can be enforced in court, and the Supreme Court of Canada agreed in May 2026 to hear an appeal. In Cowichan Tribes (2025 BCSC 1490), the BC Supreme Court found Aboriginal title under section 35 that includes privately owned land; that ruling is under appeal. The government withdrew its suspension bill on April 13, 2026. A petition to repeal DRIPA can be signed from October 26, 2026 to January 25, 2027.

prompt.1: Many people in BC die from toxic street drugs. How should the province respond?
prompt.2: Should BC focus on keeping people who use drugs alive, on required treatment, or a mix?

context.1: Toxic street drugs kill many people in BC. Some parties want places where people can use drugs with staff nearby, and doctor-prescribed drugs to replace street drugs. Others want people with the worst addictions to be required to get treatment. Some want both.
context.2: BC runs sites where people use drugs with staff on hand. Doctors can prescribe drugs to replace street drugs, and some people are required to get treatment. From 2023 to early 2026, carrying small amounts was not a crime, but that has ended. Deaths have fallen since 2023, but the coroner has not linked the drop to any one cause.
context.3: The NDP government let its decriminalization pilot, under which people were not charged for carrying small amounts, end in 2026. It now requires people on prescribed safer supply to take each dose in front of a health worker, and it is expanding involuntary care. The Conservatives would end safer supply and expand required treatment. OneBC would also close supervised sites. The Greens would bring decriminalization back. CentreBC puts treatment first, with 650 more beds.
context.4: Drug deaths fell from 2,511 in 2023 to 1,826 in 2025, but the coroner has not linked the drop to any one cause. Researchers estimate supervised consumption sites prevented about 3,945 deaths in 2023, while police chiefs point to public disorder and prescribed drugs being passed on to others. In July 2026 the BC Supreme Court struck down the parts of the Mental Health Act used for involuntary treatment and gave the government six months to amend the law.
context.5: Drug deaths were 2,511 in 2023 and 1,826 in 2025 (preliminary), and the coroner does not attribute the decline to any one cause. Requiring witnessed dosing cut the prescribed alternatives program from over 5,000 people to about 2,200. The province has 132 involuntary care beds in progress. In July 2026 the BC Supreme Court ruled the Mental Health Act's treatment provisions unconstitutional and gave the government six months to amend them. Researchers estimate supervised sites prevented 3,945 deaths in 2023. A federal study found decriminalization was not a factor in the 2024 national decline in deaths.

prompt.1: The United States put extra taxes on many BC products. How can BC protect jobs?
prompt.2: American tariffs (extra taxes on BC goods sold there) are costing jobs. How should BC protect jobs and grow the economy?
prompt.3: With American tariffs and slow growth, what should BC's plan for the economy be?
prompt.4: The United States has put tariffs on BC lumber, metals and other goods. Which economic strategy should the province pursue?
prompt.5: The United States charges tariffs on goods outside the Canada-United States-Mexico Agreement (CUSMA), on metals and on softwood lumber. Which provincial economic strategy do you prefer?

context.1: The United States now charges extra taxes on many goods from BC, and some people have lost their jobs. Parties disagree on how to respond. Ideas include selling more natural gas, buying Canadian-made goods, helping factories, logging more, or moving away from oil and gas.
context.2: BC sells lumber, natural gas, metals and food to other countries, and American tariffs have made many of those sales harder. Sawmill jobs have fallen by about a third since 2017. Parties disagree on the answer: produce more gas and mine more, have government buy Canadian, support factories and trades, move to clean energy, or allow more logging.
context.3: The NDP government would require Canadian-made materials in public projects, double mineral exports and lend money to businesses hurt by tariffs. The Conservatives would double natural gas production and approve big projects within 120 days. CentreBC would support factories and trades training, sell more to countries other than the United States and cut rules. The Greens would allow no new oil and gas projects and stop exports of unprocessed logs. OneBC wants an oil pipeline and more logging.
context.4: Employment in BC is down 0.6% so far this year, while exports to countries other than the United States rose 16%. In 2025 the NDP government passed laws to fast-track major projects. The vote was tied, and the Speaker broke the tie in the government's favour, over objections from First Nations. The Conservatives voted against those laws but now propose their own fast-track rules. Both parties take credit for Phase 2 of LNG Canada, a liquefied natural gas (LNG) export project that got the go-ahead in September 2026.
context.5: Budget 2026 assumes US tariffs of 35% on goods not covered by the Canada-United States-Mexico Agreement (CUSMA), 50% on steel, aluminum and copper, and an extra 10% on softwood lumber. Real gross domestic product (GDP) growth of 0.9% is expected in 2026. Unemployment was 6.5% in August, and employment is down 0.6% so far this year. BC sawmill jobs have fallen 32% since 2017, while exports to countries other than the US rose 16%. In May 2025, Bills 14 and 15, which fast-track major projects, passed on a 46-46 tie broken by the Speaker. LNG Canada made its final investment decision on Phase 2 in September 2026, and both main parties claim credit for it.

context.1: In BC, people hurt in car crashes get set payments for care from ICBC, the public insurer. Most cannot sue in court, which keeps prices lower. Some parties want badly hurt people to be able to sue again. Some want private companies to compete.

context.3: In 2021 the NDP government brought in a no-fault system, which pays set care and income benefits instead of letting people sue. ICBC says drivers save about $490 a year, and basic rates are frozen. Critics say people with life-changing injuries get too little. No published estimate shows how bringing back lawsuits would change prices.
context.4: Enhanced Care began in May 2021 and replaced most lawsuits with set care and income benefits. ICBC says drivers saved about $490 a year at first renewal, and basic rates are frozen until spring 2027. Critics say people with catastrophic injuries, such as brain and spinal cord injuries, are not supported well enough. No published estimate shows how restoring lawsuits would affect premiums.
context.5: Enhanced Care, in place since May 2021, pays no-fault care-based benefits instead of court awards. ICBC reports an average saving of about $490 (28%) at first renewal and $2.7 billion in rebates, with about $5 billion in claims from before 2021 still to pay. Basic rates are frozen through spring 2027. Critics say support for catastrophic injuries is inadequate. The Conservatives' hybrid proposal is described differently in a September 29 letter and an October 7 party page, and neither gives a premium estimate. The NDP's claim that premiums would double has not been verified.

context.1: The government has used strong powers to approve homes and projects quickly. It also called this election two years early. Some like fast action. Others want more checks on government, or a new voting system. In 2018, voters chose to keep the current voting system.
context.2: The NDP government used strong powers to speed up housing and big projects, sometimes over objections from cities. It called this election two years early. In 2018, BC voters chose to keep the current voting system, where the candidate with the most votes in each riding wins. Parties now propose different rules for approvals, oversight and voting.
context.3: The NDP government passed laws that let cabinet fast-track projects, override local zoning to allow more housing, and use emergency powers in response to tariffs. It called the election two years early. In a 2018 referendum, 61% of voters rejected proportional representation, a system that gives parties seats in line with their share of the vote. Parties now propose changes to approvals, oversight and voting rules.
context.4: The NDP government used provincial zoning rules, fast-track approvals by cabinet and emergency powers to respond to tariffs. Its fast-track laws passed only because the Speaker broke a 46-46 tie. It called the election two years early, and a Leger poll found 57% disapproved. context.5: Bill 7 gave cabinet tariff response powers and passed 48-44 after Part 4, a clause letting cabinet override laws, was withdrawn and a one-year sunset added. Bill 44, the 2023 zoning law, passed under time allocation, which limits debate. The snap election was called on September 22, 2026, and Angus Reid found two-thirds said it came 'too soon'. context.1: A new SkyTrain line through Fleetwood is set to open in 2029. TransLink, which runs buses and trains in the region, will be short of money from 2028. Parties disagree on how to pay for transit, and on whether some people should ride free.
context.2: The federal and provincial governments are paying for the SkyTrain line to Fleetwood and Langley, which should open in late 2029. TransLink, the regional transit agency, will be short at least $112 million a year from 2028. Both main parties have ruled out a yearly fee on vehicles. Parties disagree on who should pay, and on free fares.
context.3: The NDP government is building the line, rules out a yearly vehicle fee and promises a 2027 law to find new money for TransLink, without saying what it would be. The Conservatives criticized the cost in 2024 but made no 2026 pledge. The Greens want free transit for people under 25 and over 65. CentreBC calls the line a priority and adds rapid buses and a transit pass credit, but says nothing on the funding gap. OneBC has no position.
context.4: The line now costs $5.996 billion, up from $4 billion in the 2022 business case. TransLink needs at least $112 million a year more from 2028. The NDP and the Conservatives both rule out a vehicle levy. The other ways to close the gap are fuel or sales taxes, tolls, a provincial subsidy or service cuts, and no party has said which it would choose.
context.5: The Surrey-Langley SkyTrain will run 16 km with eight stations, three of them in or near the riding. It is budgeted at $5.996 billion, against $4.01 billion in the 2022 business case, and $2.508 billion had been spent by April 2026. The province gave TransLink $479 million in 2024 and $312 million for 2025 to 2027, but a gap of at least $112 million a year remains from 2028. On October 2 the NDP ruled out a vehicle levy of about $150 per vehicle and promised a revenue law in 2027.

context.1: Criminals in Surrey have been threatening business owners to get money, sometimes with shootings. The province pays for police and courts. Some parties want a permanent special police unit. Some want many more police across BC. Others want tougher action on repeat offenders.

context.3: Extortion means threatening someone to get money. CentreBC would make the police task force on extortion permanent and add 60 prosecutors and 500 Mounties. The Conservatives would add about 1,000 police and justice staff across BC, but their plan does not mention extortion. The NDP government set up the task force but has made no 2026 pledge. context.4: Surrey had 133 extortion cases and 49 shots-fired incidents in 2025, and 142 cases and 21 shots-fired incidents in 2026 up to September 28. Police credit steady enforcement for the drop in shootings, but no independent analysis exists. Bill 36, the 2023 law that made Surrey replace the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) with its own police service, passed over the city's objection. context.5: Surrey Police Service (SPS) figures show 9 extortion cases and 2 shots-fired incidents in 2024; 133 cases, 49 shootings and 88 victims in 2025; and 142 cases, 21 shootings, 3 arsons and 76 victims in 2026 up to September 28. An RCMP-led task force of about 40 members has worked since September 2025, and Project E_Pursuance made arrests on October 2. Under Bill 36, the SPS became the police of jurisdiction on November 29, 2024. No completion date is published: the RCMP says November 2026 and the SPS says late 2027.

context.3: The province's $312 million subsidy carries TransLink to the end of 2027. From 2028 the agency needs at least $112 million a year more. In October the NDP government ruled out a vehicle levy and road pricing and promised a law in 2027 to find another source, without naming one. The Conservatives oppose any new tax or levy. context.4: The province gave TransLink $312 million in 2025, about half of its shortfall to the end of 2027. prompt.1: A court says a First Nation owns Richmond land with homes on it. What should happen?
prompt.2: A court recognized a First Nation's title to Richmond land with private homes. How should owners be protected and claims settled?
prompt.3: A 2025 ruling recognized Cowichan title over Richmond land with private homes. How should owners be protected and claims settled?
prompt.4: The Cowichan title ruling over Richmond land with homes is under appeal. How should owners be protected and title settled?
prompt.5: In August 2025 the BC Supreme Court recognized Cowichan Tribes' Aboriginal title over Richmond land including privately held parcels; the province, Ottawa and Richmond have appealed. Which approach to homeowners and title?

context.1: A judge decided that a First Nation owns some land in Richmond, including land under people's homes. The province is fighting that decision in a higher court. Parties disagree on how to protect the people who live there, and on how to settle these claims.
context.2: In 2025 the BC Supreme Court recognized Cowichan Tribes' title over land in Richmond, including private homes. The province, the federal government and the City of Richmond have appealed. Parties disagree on whether to promise homeowners money if their home loses value, whether to change the Indigenous rights law, and whether claims should be settled by treaty or in court.
context.3: The August 2025 Cowichan ruling recognized Aboriginal title over Richmond land that includes private homes. The province is appealing and Eby says it will 'go to the wall' for owners. CentreBC would pass a law promising owners compensation for lost value. The Conservatives and OneBC would repeal the Indigenous rights law and put property rights first. The Greens would keep the law and settle claims by negotiation. A March poll found most people would put private property first.
context.4: The Cowichan decision (BC Supreme Court, August 2025) recognized Aboriginal title over part of Richmond including privately held parcels; the province, Canada, Richmond and others have appealed. A separate 2025 Court of Appeal ruling made DRIPA obligations enforceable, and the two cases are often confused. Eby calls the rulings 'overreaching' and promises to protect owners, without a compensation law. CentreBC's homeowner guarantee would compensate owners up to assessed value and keep homes mortgageable. The Conservatives and OneBC would repeal DRIPA. The Greens would legislate how DRIPA is carried out. Angus Reid (March 2026): 65% put private property first.
context.5: Cowichan Tribes v. Canada (BC Supreme Court, August 2025) recognized Aboriginal title over land in Richmond including privately owned parcels; CentreBC's platform says about 145 private properties are affected. Cowichan Tribes, the province, Canada and Richmond have all appealed. The Court of Appeal's December 2025 Gitxaala decision made Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act duties enforceable; on April 20, 2026 Eby dropped plans to amend or suspend the Act for the spring session. On September 25 he said responding to the court 'is not up for debate'. Angus Reid, March 11 to 17, 2026 (n=499): 53% say the Act goes too far, 65% put private property rights first. OneBC's Property Rights Protection Act was defeated 40 to 48 on October 29, 2025, with Conservatives voting in favour.

prompt.1: Who should decide how many homes fit on a lot: the province or city councils?
prompt.2: The province makes cities allow several homes per lot and towers near transit. Keep that power, or give it back to councils?
prompt.3: Sixteen Metro Vancouver mayors want the 2023 density laws undone. Keep the rules, add to them, or give councils back the say?
prompt.4: Sixteen Metro Vancouver mayors asked in 2025 to repeal or revise the multi-unit, transit-area and housing-target laws. What now?
prompt.5: Bill 44 (small-scale multi-unit housing, passed 45 to 29) and Bill 47 (transit-oriented areas, 65 to 0) override municipal zoning; sixteen Metro mayors sought repeal or revision in November 2025. What now?

context.1: The province recently made cities allow more homes on each lot and taller buildings near train stations. City councils used to decide this alone. Many mayors want that power back. Parties disagree on who should decide, and on what the province should do instead.
context.2: In 2023 the province passed laws making cities allow three or four homes on most lots and tall buildings near transit, and set housing targets for cities. Sixteen Metro Vancouver mayors have asked the province to repeal or change those laws. A recent poll found slightly more people back the province than councils. Parties disagree on who should decide.
context.3: The province's 2023 laws require three or four homes on most lots, higher density near transit and housing targets for named cities. Sixteen Metro Vancouver mayors asked in November 2025 to repeal or revise them. The NDP government has kept the laws. CentreBC would keep the transit rules and add provincial approval deadlines. The Conservatives promised in 2024 to scrap the lot rule, then softened that, and have no 2026 position. The Greens voted against the lot law.
context.4: Bill 44 (small-scale multi-unit housing) and Bill 47 (transit-oriented areas) passed in November 2023, with housing target orders for named cities. In late November 2025 sixteen Metro Vancouver mayors asked Premier Eby to repeal and revise all three. A Liaison Strategies poll (September 26 to 27, 2026, n=1,000) found 43% would give the province the final say over minimum housing allowances and 37% the council. The NDP has kept the laws. CentreBC keeps transit-area density and adds a provincial approval standard. The Conservatives' 2024 platform first pledged to scrap Bill 44, then softened to a fund for willing cities; nothing in 2026. The Greens voted against Bills 44 and 46.
context.5: Bill 44 passed third reading 45 to 29 on November 29, 2023, with Furstenau, Olsen, Rustad and Banman among the nays; Bill 47 passed 65 to 0 on November 30, 2023. Housing Supply Act target orders cover named Metro municipalities. On or about November 28, 2025, sixteen mayors (including Burnaby, Richmond, Coquitlam and Delta) wrote to Eby seeking repeal and revision of all three. Liaison Strategies, September 26 to 27, 2026 (n=1,000, plus or minus 3.1): province 43%, council 37% on final say; 56% support more homes nearby. The NDP has no 2026 change; its housing pledges are tax measures. CentreBC's platform sets six-month rezoning and eight-week permit standards with one rulebook by January 1, 2028, a $125 million a year performance fund and a $240 million growth fund. OneBC has no density position.

prompt.1: Should food factories be allowed on some weaker farmland in the Fraser Valley?
prompt.2: The province proposed letting food processing plants build on some lower-quality protected farmland. What should happen?
prompt.3: The province proposed letting food plants use some lower-quality land in the Agricultural Land Reserve. What should happen?
prompt.4: A July 2026 proposal would let food processors use Class 5 to 7 reserve soil, up to 0.25% of private reserve land. What now?
prompt.5: The July 2026 proposal would let food processors build on Agricultural Land Reserve Class 5 to 7 soil, capped at 0.25% of private reserve land, with a 5% local-product minimum. Which approach?

context.1: Much of the Fraser Valley is protected farmland that can only be used for farming. The province wants to let food factories build on some of the weaker soil, so more food can be made nearby. Farm groups say the land would be lost.
context.2: Much of the Fraser Valley is in the farmland reserve, where building is limited to farm use. In July 2026 the province proposed letting food processing plants build on lower-quality reserve soil, with a cap on the area and a lower local-content rule. Business groups support it; the farmland commission and farm groups oppose it. The election paused the decision.
context.3: On July 23, 2026 the NDP government proposed letting food processors build on Agricultural Land Reserve land with poorer soil, capped at a small share of private reserve land, with the local-product minimum cut from 50% to 5%. The province says 500 to 1,000 hectares in the Lower Mainland and Fraser Valley could qualify. The Abbotsford Chamber and food manufacturers back it; the Agricultural Land Commission and the BC Agriculture Council oppose it. The election paused the decision.
context.4: The July 23, 2026 proposal would allow food processing on Agricultural Land Reserve Class 5 to 7 soil, cut the local-product minimum from 50% to 5%, and cap the total at 0.25% of the 2.1 million hectares of private reserve land. The province says the soil test excludes about 90% of Fraser Valley farmland and that 500 to 1,000 hectares could qualify. Food manufacturers, the Board of Trade and the Abbotsford Chamber support it. The Agricultural Land Commission and the BC Agriculture Council oppose it. Consultation closed September 18 and the election paused the decision. Eby calls it a food security measure; the Conservatives declined to state a position.
context.5: The July 23, 2026 proposal would let food processors build on Agricultural Land Reserve Class 5 to 7 soil, cut the local-product minimum from 50% to 5%, and cap the total at 0.25% of the 2.1 million hectares of privately owned reserve land. The province says about 90% of Lower Mainland and Fraser Valley reserve farmland fails the soil test and 500 to 1,000 hectares could qualify. Supporters include BC Food and Beverage, the Board of Trade and the Abbotsford Chamber of Commerce. The Agricultural Land Commission called it one of the most significant policy shifts in decades; the BC Agriculture Council also opposes it. Consultation closed September 18, 2026 and the election call paused the decision. Eby says it affects 0.3% of the reserve; the Agriculture Council's figure is far larger and the two do not reconcile.

context.3: BC Ferries runs under a provincial mandate, with provincial funding and a provincially set board. Cancellations, long waits and rising demand are the common complaints. In May 2025 the company picked a Chinese state-owned yard for four hybrid-electric vessels after no local yard bid. context.1: Logging has long been a big employer on the Island and the coast. A pulp mill near Duncan closed this year for lack of wood. Some of the oldest forests are off limits for now. Parties disagree on protecting versus cutting.
context.2: The Crofton pulp mill, with about 350 jobs, closed last December. The premier said limits on old-growth logging were necessary and refused to let old growth be pulped to keep the mill open. Some old forests are under temporary logging deferrals. Parties disagree on what to protect and how much to cut.
context.3: Domtar's Crofton pulp mill (about 350 jobs) closed after a December 2025 announcement. Eby said old-growth limits had raised Island fibre prices but were 'a necessary decision', and that pulping old growth to extend the mill was not an option. Old-growth deferrals from 2021 are temporary. The government's Working Forest plan would zone forests with a 45 million cubic metre goal. The Greens reject the plan; CentreBC would write it into law.
context.4: Domtar's Crofton pulp mill closed after a December 2025 announcement; Eby said old-growth restrictions had raised Island fibre prices but were 'a necessary decision', and that pulping old growth to extend the mill was not an option. Old-growth deferrals from 2021 remain temporary. The Forests minister's mandate letter sets a 45 million cubic metre harvest target while Budget 2026 projects about 30 million. On October 10 in Courtenay the NDP pledged $50 million to make the rarest deferrals permanent and help mills retrofit. The Greens would protect big-treed old growth permanently. CentreBC would legislate Working Forest zones. OneBC would raise the cut. The Conservatives have no 2026 forestry plan.
context.5: Domtar's Crofton pulp mill in the Cowichan Valley (about 350 jobs) closed after a December 2025 announcement; Eby said restrictions on old-growth harvesting had raised Island fibre prices but were 'a necessary decision', and that pulping old growth to extend the mill was not an option. The 2021 old-growth deferrals remain temporary. Minister Parmar's mandate letter sets a 45 million cubic metre target; Budget 2026 projects about 30 million; the Working Forest model's first candidate area near Campbell River was announced September 15, 2026. On October 10 in Courtenay the NDP pledged $50 million to convert deferrals of 'the most irreplaceable and rarest forests' to permanent protection, with mill retrofit support for second growth. The Greens (October 4) would implement all 14 Old Growth Strategic Review recommendations and reject the 45 million target.

prompt.2: Nanaimo's hospital still waits for its new tower, and care-home projects were paused. What should come first for seniors' care?
prompt.3: Nanaimo's hospital tower and cardiac lab are only in planning, and a Campbell River care home was paused. What should come first?

prompt.5: Budget 2026 funded only concept planning for Nanaimo's tower and cath lab, paused a 153-bed Campbell River care home, and about 1,600 patients province-wide wait in hospital for care beds. Which approach?

context.1: The Island has the oldest population in the province. Nanaimo has waited years for a bigger hospital. A care home in Campbell River was put on hold, and seniors wait in hospital beds for a care home place. Parties disagree on what to build first.
context.2: The government promised Nanaimo a new hospital tower and heart lab in 2024, but the 2026 budget paid only for planning. The same budget paused seven care-home projects, including a 153-bed home in Campbell River. In October the government promised to restart them. Parties disagree on what comes first.
context.3: The NDP's 2024 pledge of a tower and cardiac lab at Nanaimo's hospital got only planning money in Budget 2026. The same budget paused seven long-term care builds, including a 153-bed facility in Campbell River. In October the NDP promised to restart the seven and put $90 million into a campus of care at the former Oak Bay Lodge. The Conservatives would let care funding follow seniors to private providers; CentreBC would cut seniors stuck in hospital.
context.4: The NDP's 2024 pledge of a patient tower and cardiac catheterization lab at Nanaimo Regional General Hospital was absent from the 2025 budget; Budget 2026 funds only initial planning. Budget 2026 also paused seven long-term care builds including a 153-bed Campbell River facility. The NDP (October 5 to 6) would restart the seven and spend $90 million on an Oak Bay Lodge campus of care. The Conservatives (October 9) would give waiting seniors portable public funding usable at non-government providers. CentreBC would cut patients stuck in hospital awaiting care from about 1,600 to 1,000 by 2030. No party has a 2026 commitment on the Nanaimo tower.
context.5: The NDP's 2024 pledge of a patient tower and cardiac catheterization lab at Nanaimo Regional General Hospital was not in the 2025 budget; Budget 2026 funds initial planning only, the ministry says concept planning takes up to 18 months, and the Nanaimo Regional Hospital District agreed to front $50 million. Budget 2026 paused seven long-term care projects including a 153-bed Campbell River facility, to adopt a lower-cost uniform design. The NDP pledges to restart the seven, $90 million toward an Oak Bay Lodge campus of care, scanners and rural recruitment incentives. The Conservatives (October 9) would give waiting seniors portable public funding at any qualified provider and cut design rules. CentreBC would cut patients awaiting long-term care in hospital from about 1,600 to 1,000 by 2030. The Greens want community health centres and public-only funding.

context.1: A huge fire near Summerland this summer forced thousands of people from their homes and destroyed many houses. The province fights fires, pays for prevention work around towns, and helps people rebuild. Parties disagree on what to spend the next money on.
context.2: The Bald Range fire started near Summerland on August 7. About 20,000 people were ordered out of Summerland and Peachland, one person died, and about 150 buildings were damaged or destroyed, many of them uninsured. context.3: The Bald Range fire began northwest of Summerland on August 7, 2026; all of Summerland and part of Peachland were evacuated, one woman died and about 150 structures were lost before it was held on August 28. In January the FireSmart community grant program closed its intake for lack of money; the 2026 budget later added $15 million. The NDP offers rebuilding help, the Conservatives aircraft, CentreBC guaranteed grants, the Greens long-term restoration funding. OneBC has no position.
context.4: The Bald Range fire (August 7 to 28, 2026) burned about 25,000 hectares northwest of Summerland; a provincial state of emergency on August 8 ordered about 20,000 residents of Summerland and Peachland out, one 80-year-old woman died, and about 150 structures were damaged or destroyed, many uninsured. The FireSmart Community Funding program closed its 2026 intake on January 30 for lack of funds; Budget 2026 then added $15 million and the 2027 intake opened October 1. Fire management was budgeted at $235.7 million for 2026/27 with spending forecast at $850 million by September. Prevention, aircraft, grants and recovery compete for the next dollar.
context.5: The Bald Range fire started August 7, 2026 about 15 km northwest of Summerland; a provincial state of emergency followed on August 8 with evacuation orders for about 20,000 people in Summerland and the Peachland area. One 80-year-old woman died while evacuating, about 150 structures were damaged or destroyed, and the fire was held on August 28 at about 25,000 hectares. Many owners were uninsured or underinsured. The Union of BC Municipalities reported in January 2026 that the FireSmart Community Funding intake closed on January 30 for lack of funds; Budget 2026 added $15 million for core FireSmart. Fire management: $235.7 million voted for 2026/27, $850 million forecast as of September 14. On October 2 the Conservatives released a wildfire plan in the Okanagan and Eby announced recovery support in Summerland.

context.4: Kelowna council's September 1 letter asked Health Canada to deny the 2027 renewal of the Pandosy Street supervised consumption site, citing 3,466 RCMP calls since 2021, and repeated its request to the province for 'a regional mandatory care facility within the Okanagan'. prompt.2: Northern mills are closing, and companies blame a shortage of wood. How should the province decide how much timber is cut?

prompt.4: Northwood pulp mill is closing over fibre supply; the province aims for 45 million cubic metres a year. How should harvest be set?

context.1: Forestry is a main employer in many northern towns. Several mills have closed, and the companies say they cannot get enough wood. The province owns most of the forest and decides how much can be cut. Parties disagree on cutting more, less, or planning differently.
context.2: Canfor announced in July that it will close its Northwood pulp mill in Prince George by the end of 2026, blaming losses and a shortage of wood fibre. The province owns most forest land and sets how much can be cut. The government wants to raise the harvest with a new zoning plan. Parties disagree on how much to cut.
context.3: Canfor announced on July 14, 2026 that its Northwood pulp mill in Prince George will close, citing pulp losses and limited fibre supply. The province's Working Forest plan would split public forest into timber, multiple-use and conservation zones with a goal of 45 million cubic metres a year, up from about 30 million. The Greens reject the plan, CentreBC would write it into law, OneBC would raise the cut, and the Conservatives have published no 2026 forestry policy.
context.4: Canfor announced on July 14, 2026 the permanent closure of the Northwood pulp mill in Prince George in the fourth quarter, about 300 direct jobs, citing pulp losses and limited BC fibre supply; West Fraser closed its 100 Mile House mill in late 2025. The Council of Forest Industries counts about 15,000 forestry jobs lost since 2022. The government's Working Forest Landscape Model would zone public forest into Working Forest, Multiple Use and Conservation areas with a 'no net loss' rule and a 45 million cubic metre annual harvest objective; the 2025 harvest was about 29 million. The first candidate area, near Campbell River, was announced September 15.
context.5: Canfor announced on July 14, 2026 that the Northwood pulp mill in Prince George will close late this year, affecting about 300 employees, citing pulp losses and limited fibre supply. The Council of Forest Industries counts about 15,000 forestry jobs lost since 2022. The Working Forest Landscape Model would zone public forest into Working Forest, Multiple Use and Conservation areas, with a 'no net loss' provision, 'to stabilize an economic land base that contributes to an annual harvest of 45 million cubic metres'; CentreBC puts the 2025 harvest at 29 million and the Ancient Forest Alliance at roughly 30 million. The first candidate area, near Campbell River, was announced September 15. Party harvest claims (a 'traditional' 60 million; 45 million as a 50% increase) conflict and are not used here.

prompt.1: Gas plants, mines and a power line are planned up north. How should they be approved?
prompt.2: Kitimat's gas export plant is doubling, and more plants, mines and a power line are proposed. How should the province handle them?
prompt.3: Kitimat's gas export plant is doubling, and more plants, mines and a power line are proposed. What conditions should apply?
prompt.4: LNG Canada is doubling; Ksi Lisims LNG, new mines and the North Coast power line await approval. What conditions should apply?
prompt.5: LNG Canada Phase 2 took its final investment decision September 29, 2026, doubling capacity; Ksi Lisims LNG, critical mineral mines and the North Coast Transmission Line await provincial decisions. Which approval approach?

context.1: The north has big projects waiting: gas export plants, new mines, and a long power line to run them. The province decides whether and how fast to approve them, and what pollution and First Nations rules apply. Parties disagree on speed and conditions.
context.2: In September the companies behind the Kitimat gas export plant agreed to build a second phase. Another gas plant near Prince Rupert, new mines, and a north coast power line are waiting on provincial decisions. The province sets approval timelines, pollution rules, the carbon price for industry, and First Nations partnership rules. Parties disagree on speed and conditions.
context.3: The Kitimat gas export plant's owners are doubling it after a September decision. The Ksi Lisims plant near Prince Rupert awaits a decision, mine proposals are in the permit queue, and the North Coast power line would supply them. The NDP requires new plants to be net-zero ready by 2030. The Conservatives would legislate 120-day approvals and drop emissions limits. CentreBC would set a one-year legal deadline. The Greens would approve no new gas plants.
context.4: LNG Canada announced its Phase 2 final investment decision on September 29, doubling Kitimat capacity to 28 million tonnes. The NDP requires new projects to be net-zero ready by 2030, would run assessments and permits at the same time, double mineral exports and fast-track the North Coast line with Canadian steel. The Conservatives' plan doubles gas production by 2032, ends emissions limits, legislates 120-day permits and sets a fixed deadline for the line. CentreBC backs LNG with First Nations partners and net-zero plans, a 12-month decision deadline and ten mine decisions by 2030. The Greens would end approvals for new LNG and pipelines.
context.5: LNG Canada's Phase 2 final investment decision (September 29, 2026) doubles Kitimat capacity to 28 million tonnes. On the NDP's own numbers, capacity reaches nearly 48 million tonnes by 2035, above the Conservatives' 'triple by 2035' target, so the real dispute is conditions and process. The NDP pledges to double critical mineral exports in five years, run permits concurrently, build the North Coast Transmission Line with Canadian steel, and keep the net-zero-ready requirement. The Conservatives would double gas by 2032 and triple by 2035, end emissions limits, pass a 120 Day Permitting Act and fix a line deadline. CentreBC requires First Nations partners and credible net-zero plans, keeps industrial carbon pricing, sets a 12-month provincial deadline and promises decisions on 10 mines by 2030. The Greens would approve no new LNG or pipelines.

text.5: Platform (October 10, Economy and Affordability): back LNG with First Nations partners and a credible net-zero-ready plan; industrial carbon pricing kept, no consumer carbon tax; BC Hydro expanded by at least 2,000 megawatts by 2033; one coordinated review with a 12-month provincial decision deadline; permitting decisions on 10 new mines by 2030 and 3 processing facilities by 2032; $1.5 billion federal ask for Prince Rupert and Roberts Bank matched by $750 million provincial road and rail over five years; Canadian steel pressed for Phase 2.

text.1: This party would approve the projects and an oil pipeline to the coast without long consultations, and cut fees.
text.3: OneBC would approve a pipeline to the Port of Prince Rupert or Kitimat 'to get Canadian energy to foreign markets', push major projects through without consultations it says act as vetoes, cut fees and approval times for mining and forestry, and work with Alberta and Saskatchewan. It has no LNG-specific, emissions or transmission position.
text.5: Priorities page: 'Approve a pipeline to the Port of Prince Rupert or Kitimat to get Canadian energy to foreign markets'; speed up permit approvals and consultations for forestry. X (September 26): major projects approved without 'consultations' that act as vetoes. October 5 post: make forestry and mining competitive with lower fees and faster approvals. No position on LNG Canada Phase 2, Ksi Lisims, emissions rules, carbon pricing or the North Coast Transmission Line; option e combines the published items.

questions.scoring_rationale: This question scores the approval process and conditions for named northern projects; the province-wide climate and economy questions score carbon pricing, targets and tariff response. a = Green (4); all others 0 (every other party backs LNG Canada Phase 2 and new mines). b = NDP (4): net-zero-ready rule, concurrent permits, North Coast line with Canadian steel, mineral exports; CentreBC 3 (same conditions and a comparable speed-up, but through a legislated deadline); Conservative 2 (backs the projects and the line, rejects the emissions conditions); Green 1 (the Canadian steel and conditions framing only); OneBC 1. c = CentreBC (4); NDP 3 (same First Nations and net-zero conditions, no legislated deadline or mine count); Conservative 2 (legislated deadline overlaps, conditions do not); OneBC 1; Green 0. d = Conservative (4); OneBC 3 (shares speed, pipelines and no emissions conditions, no production target); NDP 1 (also fast-tracks the line, keeps emissions rules); CentreBC 1 (legislated deadline, keeps conditions); Green 0. e = OneBC (4); Conservative 2 (pipeline support and speed overlap; does not reject consultation); others 0. Cross-scores on every pair of homes are within one point.

prompt.1: Emergency rooms in northern towns keep closing for lack of staff. What would help most?
prompt.2: Emergency rooms in Fort St. James, Mackenzie and Hudson's Hope keep closing for lack of staff. What would help most?
prompt.3: Emergency rooms in Fort St. James, Mackenzie, Hudson's Hope and 100 Mile House keep closing for lack of staff. What comes first?
prompt.4: Northeast BC had 115 hours of emergency and maternity closures in March 2026; 100 Mile House announced 39. What comes first?
prompt.5: Northern Health recorded 115 hours of emergency or maternity closures in the northeast in March 2026; Fort St. James and Mackenzie closed in May; 100 Mile House announced 39 closures. Which approach?

context.1: In many northern towns the hospital emergency room shuts for hours or days because no doctor or nurse can staff it. People drive long distances for help. The province pays for hospitals and decides how to attract staff. Parties disagree on what would work fastest.
context.2: Small northern hospitals closed their emergency rooms repeatedly in 2026 because of staff shortages, including Fort St. James, Mackenzie, Hudson's Hope, Chetwynd and 100 Mile House. In March the northeast lost 115 hours of emergency and maternity care. The province has opened hospitals in Terrace and Fort St. James, but staffing them is the problem. Parties disagree on the fix.
context.3: Northern Health reported 115 hours of emergency or maternity closures in northeast BC in March 2026, including 60 hours at Hudson's Hope, citing staffing. Fort St. James and Mackenzie both closed on May 26, and 100 Mile House has announced 39 closures this year. The Conservatives launched a $50 million rural fund in 100 Mile House on October 5. CentreBC promises a closure-reporting law and a yearly fund. The NDP offers tuition and moving help for rural work.
context.4: Northern Health logged 115 hours of emergency or related closures in northeast BC in March 2026 (Hudson's Hope 60), citing staffing. Fort St. James and Mackenzie closed on May 26; 100 Mile House has announced 39 closures in 2026. New hospitals opened in Terrace (2024), Fort St. James (2025) and Prince Rupert (2025), but staffing drives the closures. The Conservatives launched a $50 million rural practice fund with flexible staffing in 100 Mile House on October 5. CentreBC promises an accountability law and a $25 million a year fund. The NDP offers rural tuition, loan forgiveness and moving support. The Greens want community health centres; OneBC private care alongside public.
context.5: Northern Health reported 115 hours of emergency or related closures in northeast BC in March 2026, including 60 at Hudson's Hope, with staffing the stated cause. Fort St. James and Mackenzie closed on May 26, and 100 Mile House has announced 39 closures in 2026. The Conservatives pledge a $50 million rural practice fund, flexible staffing, automatic credential recognition and an expert commission (October 5, 100 Mile House); CentreBC an Emergency Room Accountability Act, halved unplanned closure hours by 2029/30, a $25 million a year fund and a permanent retention bonus; the NDP rural tuition discounts, loan forgiveness, moving costs and 1,000 seats (October 9); the Greens a community health centre per riding and a single authority; OneBC private care alongside public.

text.4: Publicly report every closure, halve unplanned closure hours by 2029/30, spend $25 million a year on rural locums and backup, and make the retention bonus permanent.
text.5: Enact an Emergency Room Accountability Act requiring public reporting of every closure, halve unplanned closure hours by 2029/30, fund a $25 million a year rural stabilization fund for locums, travel and virtual backup, and make the rural retention bonus permanent.

text.1: This party is in charge now. It offers cheaper tuition and moving money to bring doctors to rural areas.
text.3: The NDP government opened new hospitals in Terrace, Fort St. James and Prince Rupert, but the closures happened under it. questions.scoring_rationale: a = CentreBC (4): accountability law, halved closure hours, $25 million a year fund, permanent retention bonus; Conservative 3 (its $50 million fund does the same job without the reporting law or targets); NDP 2 (runs a rural retention incentive and built northern hospitals, but no dedicated fund or law); Green 1; OneBC 1. b = Conservative (4); CentreBC 3 (a yearly fund and faster credentials, no expert commission or staffing-rule change); NDP 2 (no fund, but fast-tracks credentials and holds the budget); Green 1; OneBC 2. c = NDP (4); Conservative 3 and CentreBC 3 (both fast-track credentials and add training; neither offers tuition or moving incentives); Green 2; OneBC 1. d = Green (4); NDP 2 and CentreBC 2 (team-based clinics and limits on agency nurses, no single authority); Conservative 0; OneBC 0. e = OneBC (4); Conservative 1 (expert commission may study other systems but keeps the system public); others 0. The Fraser Valley question on Mission's emergency room uses the same options and scores; emergency room closures ranked second in both regions' research and no region sees both questions.

scoring_method.3: Your candidate match is your party match, recalculated with the three Surrey-Fleetwood questions counting double. There is no separate candidate score; no evidence exists to build one.
scoring_method.5: Candidate alignment reuses party scores. The three Surrey-Fleetwood questions count double on top of the importance weight; provincial questions count once. Questions without a published party position are left out for that candidate. No candidate-specific adjustment: Brar never broke ranks in 105 divisions; the challengers have no record or local positions. CentreBC scores follow its October 10 platform.

local.formula: local_alignment(c) = sum over answered questions q of ( w_q * m_q * s_q(party(c)) ) / sum over answered questions q of ( w_q * m_q * 4 ). w_q = importance weight (low 0.5, medium 1, high 2). m_q = 2 if q.scope == 'local' else 1. s_q(P) = scores[P] of the chosen option. Skipped questions are excluded from both sums. Questions where party_positions[party(c)].no_position is true are excluded from both sums for that candidate only (no published position), so denominators differ by candidate. candidate_adjustment = 0 for all five candidates. Family local score = mean of members' local_alignment per candidate.

results_history.note: Margin is 751 per the Elections BC figures as reported by Wikipedia (Gill 9,172), which reconcile with the 20,416 valid votes; Stephen Taylor's site shows Gill at 9,170 (753). BC United ran no candidate.
Turnout 59.5%; runner-up Peter Fassbender (BC Liberal), who had won the seat in 2013 by about 200 votes.

competitiveness.3: NDP-held since 2017. Its margin fell from 30 points in 2020 to under 4 (751 votes) in 2024, as the Conservatives took most former BC Liberal votes. Five parties are on the 2026 ballot, up from three.
competitiveness.5: 2013: Fassbender (Liberal) 45.4%, Brar 44.4%. 2017: Brar +16.9. 2020: Brar +30.2 (60.9%). 2024: Brar +3.7 (9,923 to 9,172; one secondary site shows 9,170). 2026 ballot: five parties (three in 2024). No riding poll exists. The 2023 boundary change was minor, so results are broadly comparable.

polls_projection.3: No riding poll exists. 338Canada's model (October 9) rates it a toss-up: Conservatives 45%, NDP 42%, Greens 9%, with 8-point error margins on both leaders. That projects from province-wide polls, which disagree (Conservatives up 8 to NDP up 2).
polls_projection.5: 338Canada (October 9): toss-up; CPBC 45 (+/-8), NDP 42 (+/-8), BCG 9; win odds 65-35. PoliWave: Conservatives 45%, 1.9-point lead, 61% win chance. Provincial polls September 23 to October 8 (decided): Angus Reid Con 48, NDP 43; Liaison Con 43, NDP 37; Leger Con 39, NDP 36; Pollara tied 38; Innovative NDP 41, Con 39. Spread exceeds sampling error.

how_to_vote.voting_day: Saturday, October 24, 2026, 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. Pacific time.
how_to_vote.advance_voting: Friday October 16 to Wednesday October 21, 2026, 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. local time. Not every location is open every day; check yours.
how_to_vote.mail_in: Request a vote-by-mail package online or by phone by October 18. Elections BC must receive it by 8 p.m. Pacific time on October 24; mailing it that day is too late. Unregistered voters must include ID copies.
how_to_vote.eligibility: Canadian citizen, 18 or older on October 24, 2026, and a BC resident since April 23, 2026.
how_to_vote.id_rules: Prove identity and address one of three ways: (1) one government photo ID with your name and address (BC driver's licence, BCID, BC Services Card with photo, Certificate of Indian Status, or another government card with name, photo and address); (2) two documents with your name, at least one with your current address (electronic accepted, handwritten generally not); (3) a registered voter from your district or a close relative vouches for you.
how_to_vote.where: Find advance and election-day locations with the voting-place lookup on elections.bc.ca. District electoral offices also take voters until 4 p.m. on October 24. The October 17 municipal election is a separate vote with its own locations.
how_to_vote.other_dates: Municipal elections October 17, 2026. Televised leaders' debate October 14 (Eby, Doerkson, Lowan). Final count November 6 to 10.

kid_note.1: You must be 18 to vote. Younger people can still help their family think it through and go along to the voting place. Voting is private, so each person chooses whether to share how they voted.
